title: Reconnection Framework Glossary
description: Concepts from the Reconnection Framework: classification of polygons and polyhedra by whether their expansion families reconnect into a globally consistent adjacency graph.

expansion-family.summary: The set of all tile copies obtained by iterated application of edge-reflections, edge-half-turns, or face-reflections to a seed polygon or polyhedron.
expansion-family.definition:
Given a seed polygon (or polyhedron) $P_0$ and a **generator set** $\{g_1, \dots, g_k\}$ of edge-reflections, edge-half-turns, or face-reflections, the **expansion family** is the set

$$\mathcal{F} = \{ g_{i_1} \circ g_{i_2} \circ \cdots \circ g_{i_m}(P_0) : m \geq 0,\; i_j \in \{1, \dots, k\} \}$$

of all tile copies obtained by iterated application. Each generator corresponds to "crossing" an edge (or face) into a neighboring tile copy.

examples.title: Square expansion family
examples.body: Starting from a unit square $P_0$, applying edge reflections across each of its four sides generates the standard square tiling of the plane. The expansion family is the full set of unit squares in $\mathbb{Z}^2$.

examples.title: Pentagon expansion family
examples.body: Starting from a regular pentagon, applying edge reflections generates an infinite family of pentagons. Because the interior angle ($108°$) does not divide $360°$ evenly, the family does not close into a flat tiling but instead lives on a multi-sheeted cover.

formulas.expression: \mathcal{F} = \{ g_{i_1} \circ g_{i_2} \circ \cdots \circ g_{i_m}(P_0) : m \geq 0,\; i_j \in \{1, \dots, k\} \}
formulas.description: The expansion family as the orbit of the seed polygon under all finite compositions of generators.

seed-polygon.summary: The initial polygon or polyhedron $P_0$ from which an expansion family is generated by iterated application of generators.
seed-polygon.definition: The **seed polygon** $P_0$ is the starting tile from which the entire expansion family is built. All tile copies in the expansion family are images of $P_0$ under some composition of generators. The geometric and algebraic properties of $P_0$ — its interior angles, edge lengths, and coordinate field — determine the reconnection level of the resulting family.

examples.title: Regular pentagon as seed
examples.body: The regular pentagon with interior angle $108°$ serves as the paradigmatic Level 1 seed polygon. Its angular deficit of $36°$ prevents flat tiling but allows multi-sheeted reconnection.

examples.title: Unit square as seed
examples.body: The unit square with interior angle $90°$ is a Level 0 seed: its expansion family closes into the standard square tiling of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

generator-set.summary: The set of edge-reflections, edge-half-turns, or face-reflections whose iterated application produces the expansion family from a seed polygon.
generator-set.definition:
A **generator set** $\{g_1, \dots, g_k\}$ consists of involutions — each $g_i^2 = \mathrm{id}$ — associated to the edges (in 2D) or faces (in 3D) of the seed polygon $P_0$. The generators are:

- **Edge reflections (2D)**: reflection $r_e$ across the line containing edge $e$.
- **Edge half-turns (2D)**: half-turn $h_e$ about the midpoint of edge $e$ (orientation-preserving).
- **Face reflections (3D)**: reflection across the plane of face $f$.
- **Edge half-turns (3D)**: half-turn about the axis along edge $e$.

The choice between reflections and half-turns determines whether the tiling has orientation-reversing symmetry.

examples.title: Square generators
examples.body: The unit square has four edge reflections: across its top, bottom, left, and right edges. These four involutions generate the full square tiling symmetry group.

examples.title: Active vs. inactive edges
examples.body: In Level 2 (edge-restricted reconnection), only a subset $E_A$ of edges is active. The generator set is restricted to $\{g_e : e \in E_A\}$, and the inactive edges $E_I = E \setminus E_A$ carry additional structure but do not generate the expansion family.

formulas.description: Each generator is an involution.

adjacency-graph.summary: The graph whose vertices are tile copies in the expansion family, with edges between tiles related by a single generator; its cycle structure determines the reconnection level.
adjacency-graph.definition:
The **adjacency graph** $\mathcal{G}$ has:
- **Vertices**: tile copies in the expansion family $\mathcal{F}$.
- **Edges**: pairs of tiles related by a single generator (i.e., sharing an active edge or face).

The central question of the reconnection framework is whether $\mathcal{G}$ has many cycles (a "lattice-like" structure) or is an infinite tree:
- **Reconnection**: $\mathcal{G}$ contains cycles.
- **Non-reconnection**: $\mathcal{G}$ is an infinite tree.

The adjacency graph is essentially the **Cayley graph** of the group $\langle g_1, \dots, g_k \rangle$ (with the seed $P_0$ as identity), modulo the action on the tile.

examples.title: Square tiling adjacency graph
examples.body: For the square tiling, $\mathcal{G}$ is the infinite 2D grid graph $\mathbb{Z}^2$, which has abundant cycles. This corresponds to Level 0 (full reconnection).

examples.title: Tree adjacency graph
examples.body: For a generic irregular polygon (Level 3), $\mathcal{G}$ is an infinite 4-regular tree (for a quadrilateral). No two distinct generator words produce the same tile, so there are no cycles.

reconnection.summary: The property that the adjacency graph of an expansion family contains cycles, indicating that distinct generator words can produce the same tile copy.
reconnection.definition:
**Reconnection** occurs when the adjacency graph $\mathcal{G}$ of an expansion family contains cycles — equivalently, when two distinct compositions of generators $g_{i_1} \circ \cdots \circ g_{i_m}$ and $g_{j_1} \circ \cdots \circ g_{j_l}$ map the seed $P_0$ to the same tile copy.

**Non-reconnection** is the opposite: $\mathcal{G}$ is an infinite tree, and all generator words produce distinct tiles.

Reconnection is the central organizing concept of the framework, and its presence or absence — and the manner in which it occurs — defines the four-level hierarchy.

examples.title: Square: full reconnection
examples.body: Moving right twice and up twice from the seed square returns to the same tile as moving up twice and right twice. The adjacency graph has 4-cycles everywhere.

examples.title: Pentagon: multi-sheeted reconnection
examples.body: The pentagon's expansion family reconnects only after passing to a 10-sheeted cover. Cycles exist in $\mathcal{G}$, but they involve sheet transitions tracked by $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ labels.

reconnection-hierarchy.summary: The four-level classification of polygons and polyhedra by how their expansion families reconnect: Level 0 (flat tiling), Level 1 (multi-sheeted), Level 2 (edge-restricted), Level 3 (non-reconnective).
reconnection-hierarchy.definition:
The **reconnection hierarchy** classifies polygons and polyhedra into four levels based on the behavior of their expansion families:

- **Level 0 — Full Reconnection**: The expansion family closes into a single-sheeted Euclidean tiling of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
- **Level 1 — Multi-Sheeted Full Reconnection**: Reconnection holds after passing to a multi-sheeted covering space; angular deficit is absorbed into sheet-transition holonomy.
- **Level 2 — Edge-Restricted Reconnection**: Full reconnection fails with all edges active, but holds when restricted to a chosen subset $E_A$ of edges.
- **Level 3 — Non-Reconnective**: The expansion family is an infinite tree; no two distinct generator words produce the same tile.

This hierarchy is the **organizing principle** of the project, connecting classical crystallography (Level 0), multi-sheeted covers and discrete gauge fields (Level 1), pinwheel statistics (Level 2), and generic polygons (Level 3).

examples.title: 2D examples by level
examples.body: Level 0: square ($90°$, $\delta=0$), equilateral triangle ($60°$, $\delta=0$), regular hexagon ($120°$, $\delta=0$). Level 1: regular pentagon ($108°$, $\delta=36°$). Level 2: Conway–Radin pinwheel triangle. Level 3: generic irregular polygons, heptagon.

examples.title: 3D examples by level
examples.body: Level 0: cube ($90°$ dihedral), truncated octahedron. Level 1: octahedron (via tet-oct honeycomb), dodecahedron ($116.57°$, fiber group $2I$). Level 3: tetrahedron (irrational $\pi$ multiple).

level-0-full-reconnection.summary: The expansion family closes into a single-sheeted Euclidean tiling of $\mathbb{R}^n$; requires finite orientation group, single algebraic extension, and zero angular deficit.
level-0-full-reconnection.definition:
**Level 0 (Full Reconnection)** is the case where the expansion family closes into a **single-sheeted Euclidean tiling** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ — a standard crystallographic tiling.

**Conditions** (all three required):
1. Orientation group $\Gamma$ is finite.
2. All coordinates lie in a single algebraic extension $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$.
3. Angular deficit $\delta = 0$ at every vertex.

**Examples**:
- Square (interior angle $90°$, $\delta = 0$, field $\mathbb{Q}$).
- Equilateral triangle (interior angle $60°$, $\delta = 0$, field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$).
- Regular hexagon (interior angle $120°$, $\delta = 0$, field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$).
- Cube and tetrahedron-octahedron honeycomb in 3D.

examples.title: Square tiling
examples.body: The unit square has interior angle $90°$. Four squares meet at each vertex: $4 \times 90° = 360°$, so $\delta = 0$. The expansion family is the standard $\mathbb{Z}^2$ square tiling.

examples.title: Hexagonal tiling
examples.body: The regular hexagon has interior angle $120°$. Three hexagons meet at each vertex: $3 \times 120° = 360°$, so $\delta = 0$. The expansion family is the standard hexagonal tiling, with coordinates in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$.

formulas.description: Zero angular deficit condition required for Level 0.

level-1-multisheeted-reconnection.summary: Reconnection holds after passing to a multi-sheeted covering space; the angular deficit is absorbed into sheet-transition holonomy at vortex vertices.
level-1-multisheeted-reconnection.definition:
**Level 1 (Multi-Sheeted Full Reconnection)** is the case where reconnection holds, but only after passing to a **multi-sheeted covering space**. The angular deficit is absorbed into **sheet-transition holonomy** at vortex vertices.

**Conditions**:
1. Orientation group $\Gamma$ is finite.
2. All coordinates lie in a single algebraic extension $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$.
3. Angular deficit $\delta \neq 0$, but the lift to the covering space closes.

**Examples**:
- **Regular pentagon** (interior $108°$, deficit $36°$, fiber group $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$).
- **Regular dodecahedron** in 3D (fiber group related to binary icosahedral $2I$).
- Other regular $n$-gons with $n$ such that $\pi - 2\pi/n$ is a rational multiple of $\pi$.

examples.title: Regular pentagon
examples.body: Interior angle $108°$, deficit $36°$. Three pentagons at a vertex give $3 \times 108° = 324°$, leaving a $36°$ gap. The expansion family lives on a 10-sheeted cover with fiber group $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$.

examples.title: Regular dodecahedron
examples.body: In 3D, the dodecahedron has dihedral angle $\approx 116.57°$. Its multi-sheeted reconnection involves a fiber group related to the binary icosahedral group $2I$, with coordinates in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$.

formulas.description: Non-zero angular deficit, absorbed into sheet-transition holonomy.

level-2-edge-restricted-reconnection.summary: Full reconnection fails with all edges active, but holds when restricted to a chosen subset of active edges; exemplified by pinwheel polygons.
level-2-edge-restricted-reconnection.definition:
**Level 2 (Edge-Restricted Reconnection)** is the case where full reconnection **fails** with all edges/faces active, but reconnection **holds** when restricted to a chosen subset $E_A$ of edges/faces. These are the **pinwheel polygons**.

**Conditions**:
1. Orientation group on $E_A$ is finite (even if $\Gamma$ on the full edge set is infinite).
2. Coordinates of active edges lie in a single algebraic extension.

The **inactive edges** $E_I = E \setminus E_A$ play the role of decorations or weak gauge couplings — they do not generate the expansion family but may carry additional structure.

**Examples**:
- **Conway–Radin pinwheel triangle** (right triangle, legs $1:2$).
- Various engineered polygons mapping to $\mathbb{Z}^2$ via Gaussian integer structure.

examples.title: Conway–Radin pinwheel triangle
examples.body: The right triangle with legs in ratio $1:2$ is the classic pinwheel example. With a restricted set of active edges, the orientation group becomes finite and the expansion family reconnects. The full edge set would give an infinite orientation group.

formulas.description: Inactive edges are the complement of the active edge set.

variables.E: Full edge set of the polygon

level-3-non-reconnective.summary: The expansion family is an infinite tree — no two distinct generator words produce the same tile; the generic case for irregular polygons.
level-3-non-reconnective.definition:
**Level 3 (Non-Reconnective)** is the case where the expansion family is an **infinite tree** — no two distinct generator words produce the same tile.

**Failure modes**:
1. **Infinite orientation group**: $\Gamma$ is infinite (irrational rotation angles).
2. **Multiple incompatible irrationalities**: coordinates require two algebraically independent extensions (e.g., $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}$).
3. **No active subset closes**: even restriction to a subset $E_A$ fails to produce reconnection.

**Examples**:
- Generic irregular polygons.
- Polygons with irrational angle ratios.
- Most "random" polygons.
- Heptagon (interior angle $\approx 128.57°$, deficit $\approx 94.3°$, infinite $\Gamma$).
- Tetrahedron in 3D (dihedral angle $\approx 70.53°$, irrational $\pi$ multiple).

examples.title: Heptagon
examples.body: The regular heptagon has interior angle $\approx 128.57°$. The rotation angle $2\pi/7$ is not a rational multiple of $\pi$ in the relevant sense, giving an infinite orientation group. The expansion family is an infinite tree.

examples.title: Generic irregular quadrilateral
examples.body: A quadrilateral with irrational angle ratios has an infinite orientation group. Its expansion family grows exponentially (tree-like), with no two generator words producing the same tile.

orientation-group.summary: The subgroup of $O(n)$ generated by the rotational parts of all generators; must be finite for reconnection to hold.
orientation-group.definition:
The **orientation group** $\Gamma \leq O(n)$ is generated by the rotational parts of all generators (reflections and half-turns squared give rotations).

**Criterion 1 for reconnection**: $\Gamma$ must be **finite**. Equivalently, all rotational angles must be **rational multiples of $\pi$** (yielding roots of unity).

**Geometric meaning**: only finitely many distinct tile orientations occur in the expansion family.

If $\Gamma$ is infinite, the expansion family contains tiles in infinitely many distinct orientations, preventing closure into any finite-sheeted cover.

examples.title: Pentagon orientation group
examples.body: The regular pentagon's generators produce rotations by multiples of $\pi/5$. The orientation group is $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ (cyclic of order 10), which is finite. This is why the pentagon is Level 1 rather than Level 3.

examples.title: Heptagon orientation group
examples.body: The regular heptagon's generators produce rotations by multiples of $2\pi/7$. Since $2/7$ is not a rational multiple of $1/2$ in the relevant sense, the orientation group is infinite, placing the heptagon at Level 3.

formulas.description: The orientation group as a subgroup of the orthogonal group.

single-irrational-base.summary: The requirement that all vertex coordinates of the seed polygon lie in a single algebraic extension $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$; a necessary condition for reconnection.
single-irrational-base.definition:
**Criterion 2 (Single Irrational Base)**: All vertex coordinates of $P_0$ must lie in a **single quadratic (or higher) extension** $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ of $\mathbb{Q}$.

**Why**: if coordinates require both $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}$, then the expansion family lives in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$, which has degree 4 over $\mathbb{Q}$ and generically produces an infinite lattice point set without natural closure.

**Examples of allowed bases**:
- $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$: square family.
- $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$: hexagonal family.
- $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$: pentagonal / icosahedral family.

If coordinates require two algebraically independent extensions, the polygon is Level 3.

examples.title: Pentagon: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$
examples.body: The regular pentagon's vertices have coordinates in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$ (since $\cos(2\pi/5) = (\sqrt{5}-1)/4$). This single extension allows the expansion family to close on a multi-sheeted cover.

examples.title: Mixed irrationalities: Level 3
examples.body: A polygon whose vertices require both $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}$ lives in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$, a degree-4 extension. The expansion family generically has no closure, placing it at Level 3.

formulas.description: All vertex coordinates must lie in a single algebraic extension.

angular-deficit.summary: The difference between $360°$ and the sum of interior angles meeting at a vertex in the expansion family; zero for flat tilings, non-zero for multi-sheeted covers.
angular-deficit.definition:
The **angular deficit** $\delta$ at a vertex of the expansion family is:

$$\delta = 360° - \sum_k \theta_k$$

where $\theta_k$ are the interior angles of the tiles meeting at that vertex.

- **$\delta = 0$**: the tiles fit flat around the vertex (Level 0).
- **$\delta \neq 0$**: there is a gap or overlap; the vertex is a **vortex** and the expansion family must pass to a covering space to close (Level 1).

In 3D, the analogue is **dihedral angle integrality**: around each edge, dihedral angles must sum to $2\pi$ for Level 0.

examples.title: Pentagon angular deficit
examples.body: Interior angle of regular pentagon: $108°$. Three pentagons at a vertex: $3 \times 108° = 324°$. Deficit: $\delta = 360° - 324° = 36° = \pi/5$.

examples.title: Square: zero deficit
examples.body: Interior angle of square: $90°$. Four squares at a vertex: $4 \times 90° = 360°$. Deficit: $\delta = 0$. Flat tiling.

examples.title: 3D dihedral angle integrality
examples.body: For the cube, dihedral angle is $90°$. Three cubes meet at each edge: $3 \times 90° = 270° \neq 360°$... but in the cubic honeycomb, four cubes meet at each edge: $4 \times 90° = 360°$. Zero deficit.

formulas.description: Angular deficit at a vertex as the gap between $360°$ and the sum of meeting interior angles.

variables.\\theta_k: Interior angle of the $k$-th tile at the vertex

formulas.description: 3D dihedral angle integrality condition for Level 0 flat reconnection.

variables.\\alpha_k: Dihedral angle of the $k$-th polyhedron at the shared edge

pentagonal-pivot.summary: The regular pentagon as the paradigmatic Level 1 case, illustrating the full machinery of multi-sheeted covers, fiber groups, sheet transitions, and spinor-like holonomy.
pentagonal-pivot.definition:
The **regular pentagon** is the paradigmatic Level 1 case and the project's main focus. Its multi-sheeted resolution illustrates the framework's full machinery.

**Key data**:
- Interior angle: $108° = 3\pi/5$.
- Angular deficit: $\delta = 36° = \pi/5$.
- Orientation group: $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ (10 distinct rotation angles).
- Fiber group: $G = \mathbb{Z}_{10}$.
- Coordinate field: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$.

The expansion family lives on a **10-sheeted cover** of the punctured plane. Each tile is labeled by an element of $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ indicating its sheet. The structure assembles into a **discrete principal $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$-bundle** over $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \Sigma$, where $\Sigma$ is the set of vortex vertices.

examples.title: Vertex deficit computation
examples.body: Three pentagons at a vertex: $3 \times 108° = 324°$. Deficit: $36°$. This $36°$ gap is the fundamental quantum of sheet transition in the 10-sheeted cover.

examples.title: Spinor-like behavior
examples.body: A loop around a vortex accumulates total sheet shift $\pm 1 \mod 10$. Five loops give $\pm 5 = 5 \mod 10$. In the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ projection (sheet parity), one loop gives a parity flip — spinor-like behavior. Ten loops restore identity.

formulas.description: Interior angle of the regular pentagon.
Angular deficit at each vortex vertex of the pentagonal expansion family.
Holonomy around a single vortex: total sheet shift is $\pm 1$ modulo 10.

multi-sheeted-cover.summary: A covering space over the punctured plane (or $\mathbb{R}^n$ minus vortex points) on which the expansion family of a Level 1 polygon closes into a globally consistent tiling.
multi-sheeted-cover.definition:
A **multi-sheeted cover** is a covering space $\tilde{X} \to X$ where $X = \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \Sigma$ (the plane or space minus the set $\Sigma$ of vortex vertices). The expansion family of a Level 1 polygon, which does not close in $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself, closes into a globally consistent tiling on $\tilde{X}$.

For the regular pentagon:
- The cover has **10 sheets** (fiber group $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$).
- Each tile copy is labeled by a sheet index in $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$.
- Crossing an edge $e$ shifts the sheet index by $\tau(e) \in \mathbb{Z}_{10}$.
- The monodromy around a vortex is $\pm 1 \in \mathbb{Z}_{10}$.

examples.title: 10-sheeted pentagon cover
examples.body: The regular pentagon's expansion family lives on a 10-sheeted cover of $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \Sigma$. Each of the 10 sheets corresponds to one of the 10 distinct tile orientations (elements of $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$).

formulas.description: The covering map from the multi-sheeted cover to the punctured space.

fiber-group.summary: The group labeling the sheets of the multi-sheeted cover; for the regular pentagon it is $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$, for the dodecahedron it is related to the binary icosahedral group $2I$.
fiber-group.definition:
The **fiber group** $G$ is the group that labels the sheets of the multi-sheeted cover. It is isomorphic to the orientation group $\Gamma$ of the expansion family.

- For the **regular pentagon**: $G = \mathbb{Z}_{10}$ (cyclic of order 10), since $\pi/5$ generates a cyclic group of order 10 under doubling.
- For the **regular dodecahedron**: $G$ is related to the binary icosahedral group $2I$.

The fiber group is the structure group of the discrete principal $G$-bundle over the punctured space.

examples.title: Pentagon fiber group $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$
examples.body: The orientation group of the pentagon is $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$: the 10 distinct rotation angles are $0, \pi/5, 2\pi/5, \ldots, 9\pi/5$. The fiber group is $G = \mathbb{Z}_{10}$, and the cover has 10 sheets.

examples.title: Dodecahedron fiber group
examples.body: The regular dodecahedron's multi-sheeted reconnection involves a fiber group related to the binary icosahedral group $2I$, reflecting the icosahedral symmetry of the 3D expansion family.

formulas.description: Fiber group for the regular pentagon.

sheet-transition-holonomy.summary: The sheet-index shift $\tau(e) \in G$ accumulated when crossing an edge $e$ in the multi-sheeted cover; its sum around a vortex gives the monodromy.
sheet-transition-holonomy.definition:
Each edge $e$ of the tiling carries a **sheet-transition label** $\tau(e) \in G$ (the fiber group). Crossing edge $e$ shifts the sheet index by $\tau(e)$.

The **signed3 rule** assigns shifts in $\{-1, 0, +1\}$ cyclically around each vortex, giving a vortex-edge fraction of exactly $2/3$.

**Holonomy around a vortex**: a loop $\gamma$ around a vortex accumulates total sheet shift:
$$\sum_{e \in \gamma} \tau(e) = \pm 1 \mod 10$$

This is the monodromy of the discrete principal bundle. Two loops give $\pm 2$; five loops give $\pm 5$; ten loops restore identity.

examples.title: Single vortex loop
examples.body: A loop around one vortex vertex of the pentagonal tiling accumulates sheet shift $+1 \in \mathbb{Z}_{10}$. After 10 loops, the sheet index returns to its starting value.

examples.title: Signed3 rule
examples.body: Around each vortex, the three meeting edges carry sheet-transition labels from $\{-1, 0, +1\}$ assigned cyclically. The sum is $-1 + 0 + 1 = 0$ locally, but the holonomy around the vortex is $\pm 1$ due to the cyclic assignment pattern.

formulas.description: Holonomy (total sheet shift) around a single vortex loop.

vortex-vertex.summary: A vertex in the expansion family where the angular deficit $\delta \neq 0$; the puncture points of the base space over which the multi-sheeted cover is built.
vortex-vertex.definition:
A **vortex vertex** is a vertex in the expansion family where the angular deficit $\delta \neq 0$ — the tiles meeting at that vertex do not fill the full $360°$. Vortex vertices are the **singular points** of the tiling.

The set $\Sigma$ of all vortex vertices is removed from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to form the base space $X = \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \Sigma$ of the multi-sheeted cover. The sheet-transition holonomy is non-trivial precisely around loops encircling vortex vertices.

examples.title: Pentagon vortex vertices
examples.body: In the pentagonal expansion family, every vertex where three pentagons meet is a vortex vertex with deficit $36°$. These are the puncture points of the 10-sheeted cover.

formulas.description: Base space of the multi-sheeted cover, with vortex vertices removed.

discrete-principal-bundle.summary: The discrete principal $G$-bundle over the punctured plane encoding the sheet structure, edge transitions, and holonomy of a Level 1 expansion family.
discrete-principal-bundle.definition:
The full structure of a Level 1 expansion family assembles into a **discrete principal $G$-bundle** over the punctured space $X = \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \Sigma$:

- **Base space**: $X = \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \Sigma$ (plane minus vortex vertices).
- **Structure group**: $G$ (the fiber group, e.g., $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ for the pentagon).
- **Total space**: the multi-sheeted cover $\tilde{X}$.
- **Connection**: the edge-transition labels $\tau(e) \in G$.
- **Curvature/holonomy**: $\pm 1 \in G$ around each vortex.

This is the discrete analogue of a gauge field in physics, with the vortex vertices playing the role of magnetic flux tubes.

examples.title: Pentagon $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$-bundle
examples.body: The pentagonal expansion family defines a discrete principal $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$-bundle over $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \Sigma$. The connection is given by the signed3 rule assigning $\tau(e) \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$ to each edge. The holonomy around each vortex is $\pm 1 \in \mathbb{Z}_{10}$.

spinor-like-behavior.summary: The phenomenon in the pentagonal expansion family where a loop around a vortex flips sheet parity (analogous to a spinor's sign change under $2\pi$ rotation), with identity restored only after ten loops.
spinor-like-behavior.definition:
The **spinor-like behavior** of the pentagonal expansion family arises from the $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ fiber group structure:

- One loop around a vortex: sheet shift $\pm 1 \in \mathbb{Z}_{10}$.
- Five loops: sheet shift $\pm 5 \equiv 5 \mod 10$.
- Ten loops: sheet shift $\pm 10 \equiv 0 \mod 10$ (identity restored).

In the **$\mathbb{Z}_2$ projection** (sheet parity = sheet index mod 2):
- One loop: parity flips (analogous to a spinor's $-1$ under $2\pi$ rotation).
- Two loops: parity restored.

This is the discrete analogue of spinor behavior: the "wavefunction" (sheet label) changes sign under a single full loop, and requires two loops to return to its original value.

examples.title: Pentagon spinor analogy
examples.body: Just as a spin-$1/2$ particle acquires a factor of $-1$ under a $2\pi$ rotation (requiring $4\pi$ for identity), a tile in the pentagonal expansion family acquires a sheet-parity flip under one vortex loop, requiring two loops for parity restoration.

formulas.description: Five vortex loops give sheet shift 5, the 'half-way' point of $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$.
Ten vortex loops restore the sheet index to its original value.

signed3-rule.summary: The rule assigning sheet-transition labels from $\{-1, 0, +1\}$ cyclically around each vortex, giving a vortex-edge fraction of exactly $2/3$.
signed3-rule.definition:
The **signed3 rule** is the assignment of sheet-transition labels $\tau(e) \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$ to edges cyclically around each vortex vertex, such that:
- The labels cycle through $(-1, 0, +1)$ around each vortex.
- The **vortex-edge fraction** (fraction of edges with non-zero label) is exactly $2/3$.

This rule ensures that the holonomy around each vortex is $\pm 1 \in \mathbb{Z}_{10}$, consistent with the discrete principal bundle structure.

examples.title: Three-edge vortex
examples.body: At a vortex where three pentagon edges meet, the signed3 rule assigns labels $(-1, 0, +1)$ to the three edges in cyclic order. Two of the three edges carry non-zero labels (fraction $2/3$).

formulas.description: Sheet-transition labels assigned by the signed3 rule.

edge-reflections.summary: Reflections across the lines containing edges of the seed polygon; orientation-reversing involutions used as generators of the expansion family.
edge-reflections.definition:
For each edge $e$ of $P_0$, the **edge reflection** $r_e$ is the reflection across the line containing $e$. It is an involution: $r_e^2 = \mathrm{id}$.

The expanded family treats $P_0$ and $r_e(P_0)$ as adjacent tiles sharing edge $e$.

Edge reflections are **orientation-reversing** (determinant $-1$). If the generator set consists entirely of edge reflections, the tiling has orientation-reversing symmetry.

examples.title: Square edge reflections
examples.body: The unit square has four edge reflections: $r_{\text{top}}, r_{\text{bottom}}, r_{\text{left}}, r_{\text{right}}$. Each reflects the square across one of its four sides, producing the adjacent square in that direction.

formulas.description: Edge reflections are involutions.

variables.r_e: Reflection across the line containing edge $e$

edge-half-turns.summary: Half-turns (180° rotations) about edge midpoints (2D) or edge axes (3D); orientation-preserving involutions used as generators of the expansion family.
edge-half-turns.definition:
**Edge half-turns** are involutions of determinant $+1$ (orientation-preserving):

- **2D**: For each edge $e$, the half-turn $h_e$ about the midpoint of $e$ is a $180°$ rotation. $h_e^2 = \mathrm{id}$.
- **3D**: For each edge $e$ of $P_0$, the half-turn about the axis along $e$ is a $180°$ rotation about that axis.

Half-turns preserve orientation; reflections reverse it. The choice between reflections and half-turns determines whether the tiling has orientation-reversing symmetry.

examples.title: Square edge half-turns
examples.body: The unit square has four edge half-turns: $180°$ rotations about the midpoints of its four sides. Each maps the square to the adjacent square sharing that edge, but without flipping orientation.

formulas.description: Edge half-turns are involutions.

variables.h_e: Half-turn about the midpoint (2D) or axis (3D) of edge $e$

cayley-graph-perspective.summary: The adjacency graph of the expansion family is essentially the Cayley graph of the generator group; polynomial growth corresponds to reconnection, exponential growth to non-reconnection.
cayley-graph-perspective.definition:
The expansion family $\mathcal{F}$ is the orbit of $P_0$ under the group
$$\langle g_1, \dots, g_k \rangle$$
generated by the generators in the affine group $\mathrm{Aff}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The adjacency graph $\mathcal{G}$ is essentially the **Cayley graph** of this group (with the seed $P_0$ as identity), modulo the action on the tile.

**Growth rates by level**:
- **Level 0–1**: the group is virtually a lattice (crystallographic); Cayley graph has **polynomial growth**.
- **Level 2**: the restricted group is virtually a lattice; full group may not be.
- **Level 3**: the group is **virtually free**; Cayley graph has **exponential growth** (tree-like).

The transition from polynomial to exponential growth in the Cayley graph **is** the transition from reconnective to non-reconnective.

examples.title: Square: polynomial growth
examples.body: The group generated by the four square edge reflections is the wallpaper group $p4m$, which is virtually $\mathbb{Z}^2$. The Cayley graph has polynomial (quadratic) growth.

examples.title: Generic polygon: exponential growth
examples.body: For a generic irregular quadrilateral, the group generated by four edge reflections is virtually free of rank 3. The Cayley graph is tree-like with exponential growth.

formulas.description: The generator group as a subgroup of the affine group.
